title: The Belay on K2
text:
In the summer of 1953 an American expedition led by Charles Houston attempted K2, the world's second highest mountain, with eight climbers. By early August they were high on the mountain at their highest camp, ready for a summit push, when a storm pinned them in their tents for days.

Then one of the climbers, Art Gilkey, collapsed. Houston, a doctor, diagnosed blood clots in his leg, a condition likely to kill him at that altitude. The summit was forgotten. The team decided to try to get Gilkey down, wrapping him in a sleeping bag and a tent and lowering him down the steep slopes in the storm.

On 10 August, during the descent, one climber, George Bell, slipped. His rope partner was pulled off, and their rope tangled with others. Within seconds five men were falling down the slope toward a drop of thousands of feet. Above them, Pete Schoening was holding the rope attached to Gilkey, with his ice axe jammed behind a boulder. When the falling ropes caught on Gilkey's line, Schoening held on. The axe held, the rope held, and all six men stopped.

Shortly afterward, while the others pitched an emergency camp, Gilkey, anchored to the slope nearby, was swept away, most likely by an avalanche. The rest of the team, injured and exhausted, made it down the mountain alive. Schoening's ice axe is preserved in a museum.
lesson: A team roped together shares its fate. Abandoning the summit to save one member, and one person's steady grip, can keep everyone alive.
people: Pete Schoening, Charles Houston, Art Gilkey, George Bell, Robert Bates
source: Charles S. Houston and Robert H. Bates, K2: The Savage Mountain (1954)
caveat: It is not known for certain whether Gilkey was taken by an avalanche or freed himself to spare the others; most accounts favor the avalanche.
